item.title: i only play one instrument (guitar) and am very interested in music, i already write poetry a lot but idk how to start. i dont really love the sound of just guitar on its on own but cant afford any other instruments, how do i get into production and actually writing artistically? whats your advice? thank you mr wurtz
item.description:
10.3.26 12:02 am
Q: i only play one instrument (guitar) and am very interested in music, i already write poetry a lot but idk how to start. i dont really love the sound of just guitar on its on own but cant afford any other instruments, how do i get into production and actually writing artistically? whats your advice? thank you mr wurtz
A: if you want to play music all by yourself, you probably already have a head start in knowing the guitar. guitar is one of the most useful instruments for playing and singing songs all by yourself. You mention you arent so fond of the guitar alone, which gives me a hint that maybe it's electric (the acoustic guitar is specifically one of the all time strongest instruments for a solo singer-songwriter), but with a little bit of experimentation i think you can find a sound that really makes sense for singing songs with. Maybe the hardest part of getting into the brave world of independent self musical expression, is that we probably always underestimate how thrilling it actually could be. this is your chance to actually let your deepest self really communicate. and before you've done it, you have no idea what it's going to say

A: yes i do, and it feels like a pretty big discovery the first time you are able to do it. but once you do it you'll probably jump through the roof you'll be so excited. Basically you wanna be like a doctor, and the item is the patient. First you have to assess the basic condition of this item. Run through it. Do you even like it? figure out what you like about it, give a general diagnosis about what you think the thing is, or could be. Part of the tricky part sometimes is dealing with the fact that you are now a slightly different person than you were then. but this can be used to your advantage. Sometimes what i find helpful, especially if it's a long time later, like years, don't just try to pick it up and pretend you're still in that exact same place. Instead, think of it like you are now writing the story of what it felt like to be in the place you were before. Sometimes when i pick these things up after years, sometimes one of the first things that gets added is like a piece of storytelling that tells a story about me writing the initial thing. it's hard to explain exactly how this works, but it is very very possible and it's extremely fun. perhaps more fun even than just writing it all at once. It really comes down to whether you believe you can do it, and once you open the door to acknowledging the difference between your current self and past self, and expressing that difference honestly, you can use it to your advantage. Once you succeed once at doing this, you'll always believe it's possible. i'll never forget when i first discovered this possibility, and now i use it with almost everything i write

item.title: It messes me up when I see low-effort brainrot works become more popular than my works that I have put my soul into. I know I probably shouldn't create art just for the sake of being popular, but seeing people appreciating that kind of work over mine is very demoralizing to me. How did you get over this toxic way of thinking?
item.description:
10.8.26 9:46 pm
Q: It messes me up when I see low-effort brainrot works become more popular than my works that I have put my soul into. I know I probably shouldn't create art just for the sake of being popular, but seeing people appreciating that kind of work over mine is very demoralizing to me. How did you get over this toxic way of thinking?
A: i surely have other toxic ways of thinking, maybe some of them worse, but i dont tend to have that one. all i can do here is try to explain what doesnt make sense to me about that viewpoint, which hopefully may be useful despite my lack of understanding. to immediately judge something to be 'brainrot', i think is terribly unfair. usually a golden rule i tend to go by is "if you dont like it, then it means you havent really seen it." secondly, it's always worth having faith that there's a major difference between short term popularity and long term popularity. maybe this requires you to have an artist sized ego, but it can be pretty handy to convince yourself that your work is meant to play a longer game. as time goes by this difference becomes more clear, or there's sort of a cheat code to realize this quicker: you can browse through things from the past and find plenty of things that sucked and got popular but didnt really last. But what also happens is, sometiems, some of the things that you hated, and surely thought would only be temporary, actually stick around for a long time. i'll admit that's weird, but you have to fall back on "youre just not seeing what other people are seeing in it." a basic phenomenon of creative work is, it hits everyone differently. from time to time i'm sure you'll have the experience of having your best friend say they CANT STAND something that you think is the most brilliant thing ever, and they may literally say it's the stupidest thing ever. plus you know they're not stupid either. And the same thing happens the other way around, where you think one of their all time favorites is stupid. fascinating, and it happens over and over again. sometimes i keep a sort of mental bookmark of the most shocking occurences of this phenomenon, to sort of benchmark just how fickle the perception of art can be. One more thing i'm also noticing in what you desecribed: you make a sort of correlation between 'effort' and 'soul'. i dont think that adds up. effort can be one of the biggest sabateurs to the soul. what's ironic is, effort always seems to come around whenever you really really care. but trying too hard almost always gets in the way. Despite knowing this, i'm not very good at avoiding it. i always try too hard, and it always has a very dampening effect on the result. "high effort" usually tends to mean it ends up feeling very stifled and suffocated. so "low effort = bad" doesnt make sense to me. if something is low effort, that means there's a good chance it came out awesome because they forgot to ruin it, and i'm jealous of both how awesome and how easy it was, as i continue along in a state of facepalm, trying so hard not to try hard

item.title: do you like a song less if it's entirely in c major
item.description:
10.16.26 12:14 am
Q: do you like a song less if it's entirely in c major
A: it all comes down to "less than what". i will list a few different scenarios. if the song was always in C, meant to be in C, then that is certainly not a negative attribute. if the song was meant to be in another key but then transposed and re-performed in C, that's not necessarily a bad thing either unless it happens to be a bad range for the singer or for the instruments in some way. If the song was recorded in another key and then pitch shifted to a new key (C), that might get kind of ugly, or it might actually sound cool with the pitch shift. If the song was written with KEY CHANGES but then was modified to keep it all in the same key but still have chord changes, within the key of C (C, F, G, Amin, Dmin, etc) then it's possible that the modified version could be worse, but it's also possible that it could be better. Then there's also a possibility that when you say "entirely in C major" you mean not just that the song is in that key but maybe you mean that every chord is C, or even more extreme, every note is C. like those viral pitch-correction experiments with 'hey now youre an allstar', or 'giant steps'. this could have some value just for being interesting, if you've never heard of that technology before. but then after the novelty wears off it wouldnt be so interesting. maybe the important thing which i should have said first, my entire answer here would be the same regardless of whether you were asking about C, Gb, or any key

item.title: What's the first step you usually take when making a new song? do you start with improv, or memo down a tune that appears in your head, or something else?
item.description:
10.21.26 12:31 am
Q: What's the first step you usually take when making a new song? do you start with improv, or memo down a tune that appears in your head, or something else?
A: here is a general list of all the different ways, and i will try to explain the mechanics behind all of them. first we have to separate it into two general catagories: when it comes to me at a totally unexpected time and place, and when i do a dedicated session trying to get things to come to me on purpose now. When it drops on my head at an unexpected time, i immediately leap to write it down. usually a combination of a memo recording and text is best to convey all the necessary specifics of how it goes. if no harmonic musical instrument is available then i can explain the whole thing with just my voice, it just takes slightly longer to make sure i clarify and explain any harmonic information i might need. and if i absolutely cannot record a memo, then i have to get it done with text alone, in which case you see a lot of number charts, for melody, chords, AND rhythm, then me explaining it every different which way multiple times, just to make sure i'm clearly clarifying how it actually sounds. not so easy with text alone, but it can be done. so anyway that's how it works when the things come at me not on a writing session. But then there's when it's an actual writing session. now, you asked about the very first part of a song, so right now i am only talking about the starting sessions, which as i said include the unexpected drop-ins, and the deliberate session. but even with those deliberate sessions, right now i'm only referring to 'new idea' sessions, not the other types of sessions such as 'middle writing' (where i 'continue' writing on things) or production (which actually starts with 'selection' then writing to completion, then recording). So the 'new idea' sessions, deliberate sessions (not when it falls on my head at some other time), with those i usually do pretty high quantity just to get things going, and i make sure to spread it around a lot of different sorts of 'strategies'. things like, start with a tempo. or start with just a couple of words. or a keyboard improv. or a vocal improv. or a textual improv. sometimes i say i'm just gonna come up with 10 cool titles. sometimes i look at an image and see if that brings something. maybe browse maps, see if that brings up anything. It's often a bit bland to get the engine started on these new idea sessions at first, so it's important to have a little patience. i've learned over the years not to panic when the first few seem lousy. it can clearly be seen from the records of past sessions, that the first few are almost always pretty lame. which is an advantage as you get older, to be able to look back on past sessions and see how it all played out. Usually starts out like, ok that one sucked, do another one, ok well that one kinda almost didnt suck, but im not sure, then another one and another one and soon enough there is one where youre like "AH ok i THINK that one probably is good for something." then do another and another and you just kind of sort of lose track of how many youve done, and when you look back on it later you find that there are more good ones in there than you realized. so this is only the 'new idea' department that i've described here, both the deliberate session and catching the unnanounced drop-ins when off session
